newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Freed U.N. plane diverts to Taleban headquarters.
newsitem.headline: Freed U.N. plane diverts to Taleban headquarters.

text.p: A U.N. plane that had been forced to land by Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban militia was released on Sunday, but then flew to Taleban headquarters in the southern city of Kandahar, a U.N. official said.
The plane, a 10-seater Beechcraft, was believed to be carrying Tajik Islamic rebel leader Sayed Abdullo Nuri on his way to a meeting with Tajik President Imamali Rakhmonov.

Alfredo Witschi-Cestari, coordinator of the U.N. Office for Humanitarian Assistance to Afghanistan, said the plane had diverted to Kandahar with a technical problem after being allowed to leave Shindand military base in western Afghanistan.
"The Danish pilots will try to repair it themselves. Otherwise they will spend the night in Kandahar and we will send a technician from Islamabad tomorrow," he told Reuters.
Witschi-Cestari could not confirm that Nuri was on the flight, which had been arranged by U.N. officials in the Tajikistan capital, Dushanbe, or identify other passengers.
U.N. sources said earlier that the plane had left the Soviet-built Shindand base, about 120 km (75 miles) south of Herat, and was bound for Kunduz in northern Afghanistan.
Taleban jets intercepted the plane, which had taken off from Mashhad in eastern Iran, and forced it to land at Shindand on Saturday, saying it had no permission to use Afghan airspace.
"We have released the plane and authorised it to fly because it is now clear that it is a U.N. plane," said a spokesman for the Taleban governor of Herat, Mullah Yar Mohammad.
"We respect the United Nations, but we request that we should be notified about any future U.N. flight," said the spokesman, contacted by telephone.
The United Nations is trying to mediate between the Islamic opposition guerrillas and Rakhmonov's Russian-backed government.
Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Rakhmonov on Saturday as saying he planned to meet Nuri early this week despite the latest flare-up in fighting in the former Soviet republic.
The Tajik government says the Islamic rebels operate from bases in northern Afghanistan. The Taleban have criticised Tajikistan in the past for alleged meddling in Afghan affairs.

The Taleban captured Shindand from forces loyal to then president Burhanuddin Rabbani in August 1995 and the western city of Herat the following month. The hardline Islamic militia drove Rabbani's government from Kabul on September 27 this year.
In August 1995 the Taleban forced a chartered cargo plane carrying weapons for Rabbani's government to land in Kandahar.
The militia held the plane's seven Russian crew captive in Kandahar for just over a year before the crew staged a dramatic escape, flying their own aircraft to the United Arab Emirates.
